newsitem.title: INDIA: India pledges no let-up in corruption battle.
newsitem.headline: India pledges no let-up in corruption battle.

text.p: The Indian government on Tuesday promised an unrelenting fight against corruption as Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral faced stiff criticism for abruptly transferring the federal police chief to a new job.
Critics accused Gujral of bowing to political pressure when he shifted Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) director Joginder Singh on Monday to the Home (Interior) Ministry.

They said the sudden decision to transfer Singh, who had led a high-profile campaign against political corruption and spearheaded a criminal probe into the chief of Gujral's party, sent the wrong signal at the wrong time.

"It was improper and open to misintepretation," Communist Party of India national secretary D. Raja told Reuters. "The prime minister should ensure that there is no interference in the CBI's work and the ongoing judicial process."
The Pioneer newspaper had sharper words.

"Maybe the prime minister has become a helpless hostage to the politics of chicanery, deceit and corruption over which he accidently presides," the newspaper's editor, Chandan Mitra, said in a front-page editorial.

Gujral's Janata Dal party faces a potential split following the indictment of its president, Laloo Prasad Yadav, in a $280-million corruption case involving alleged siphoning-off of animal welfare funds.
Yadav, who is chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, has said he is innocent and steadfastly refused to step down as either state or party leader.
The biggest group in Gujral's 15-party coalition, Janata Dal, is set to elect a leader on Thursday, and Yadav's supporters have threatened to boycott the vote and break away.
They are demanding that a Yadav ally be reinstated on a panel of poll observers, and that the voters' list be adjusted.
The upheaval in Gujral's party has shaken the ruling alliance barely two months after the prime minister assumed power following a month-long political crisis.

A government spokesman dismissed claims that Gujral had transferred Singh, who had taken over the CBI only 11 months before, to appease critics in Janata Dal and the Congress party who may want a slowdown in the corruption investigations.
"There will be no let-up in any investigation undertaken by the CBI irrespective of the status of the person, even regarding the cases in Bihar," the spokesman said.
"The present pace will continue. There will be no change."
Officials said Gujral was upset that under Singh, the CBI's cases were being played out in detail in the press but the agency was having trouble winning convictions.

They cited an $18-million money-laundering case allegedly involving more than 100 politicians and bureaucrats but which has begun to unravel for lack of evidence. Former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao was recently acquitted in a forgery case.

"The prime minister more than once has cautioned, saying not to go for publicity-oriented investigations," an official said. "We should not be conducting media trials, especially if the cases do not gel. Do the job, but do it quietly."
A piqued Singh, who was in France to attend an Interpol meeting when his transfer was announced, may not take up his new job at the Home Ministry in protest, United News of India said.
